sources_read: .qc-cache/kittle-2026-10-09-r2/rules/WebDev Rubrics QC.xlsx (quality row 44 'dimension_and_criterion_weights_are_honest': 'Weight (scoring.toml [weights] + per-criterion weights) tracks what each thing proves - real functionality is weighted above structure and style.'; internal annotation by Mukesh: functionality 60%, per-dimension own criterion weightage; neighbouring rows 42/43 on ranking and gates)
evidence: Dimension level is honest: task/tests/scoring.toml is byte-identical to the frozen template (functional 0.6, polish 0.2, visual 0.2, floor functional 0.05, gates 0.0; sha256 95f70d6e...). Function outweighs style; maximum non-functional contribution is 0.4 and requires clearing gates plus the 0.05 functional floor (template-controlled, not a task defect). Polish criteria are all 1.0 binary; visual likert weights 2.0/2.0/1.0/1.0 favour the domain-relevant matter list and retention marks over generic phone/transcript look. Criterion level is NOT consistent with the task's own documented weight scheme. scored/functional/judge.toml states: 'Core legal behaviour (walls, retention, holds, persistence) is 2.0, ordinary chat behaviour is 1.5 and a single small behaviour is 1.0; a criterion with parts takes their sum.' The brief (instruction.md line 3) says walls and retention 'matter more than anything else', and environment/instructions/conversations.md groups edits, formatting, unread and live updates as how 'we talk in a matter' i.e. ordinary chat. Yet edits_and_stale_edit=2.0, safe_formatting=2.0, unread_and_new_messages_line=2.0 and live_updates_keep_my_work=2.0 are single-part chat criteria weighted at the core-legal tier, while nested_replies and message_links (also chat) get 1.5. Conversely deleted_and_expired_messages=3.0 has a pure-retention Part B (core, 2.0 by the rule) plus a multi-step deletion/expiry Part A, so the rule implies >=3.5. Totals: legal/access/retention/hold/persistence criteria = 17.0 of 33.0 (51.5%), chat criteria = 16.0 (48.5%), so the brief's 'more than anything else' priority is barely reflected per criterion, and four chat criteria are each worth exactly as much as each wall criterion. Under the stated rule the chat block would be 14.0. No reward discrimination/ranking run exists (raw-evidence-index scope), so the effect of weights on ranking is unmeasured.
counterexample: Broken-priority app A: implements edits+stale edit, safe formatting, unread counts and live updates perfectly (4 x 2.0 = 8.0) but leaks M-12 on every wall route and through mentions/links (wall_every_route, wall_mentions_and_links fail, -4.0). Conforming-priority app B: walls perfect but unread and live updates broken. Per the documented rule A's chat set should be worth 6.0, yet it scores 8.0, equal to two full wall criteria, so an app that violates the brief's top priority gains the same functional credit as one that protects it. A customer audit recomputing against the comment's own scheme finds 4 criteria (8.0 of 33.0 mass) off-rule.
suggested_fix: Make the weights and the documented rule agree, without steering the band: either set edits_and_stale_edit, safe_formatting, unread_and_new_messages_line and live_updates_keep_my_work to 1.5 (and recheck deleted_and_expired_messages against the part-sum rule, e.g. 2.0 retention + 1.5 deletion = 3.5), or amend the weight-rule comment to name an explicit additional 2.0 class (e.g. security/authorization or concurrency-integrity behaviours) with a reason that is consistent with the brief's stated priorities, and apply it uniformly. Re-review rows 42/43/44 and recompute equal-weight vs weighted outcomes afterwards.
